utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues Ms. Paterson, Ms. MacFadyen, Ms. Hayden and Ms. Annink-Janvier, as the case manager, for the Prosecution, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Brashich for the accused Todorovic. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. Pantelic, Defence counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. de Saint Just from the Paris bar for Miroslav Tadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am Mr. Branislav Avramovic for Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Borislav Pisarevic for Simo Zaric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am Aleksandar Lazarevic, Your Honours, the legal assistant of Mr. Pisarevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to ensure that the accused are hearing the proceedings in a language which they understand. I call first on the accused Tadic. Are you hearing the proceedings, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TADIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TODOROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ZARIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a Pre-Trial Conference, and I will, at the outset, outline the matters that we will consider today and the order in which we will take them. First, there is a motion by the Prosecution for protective measures; secondly, there is a Prosecution motion in respect of judicial notice; thirdly, the question of status of disclosure of witness statements; fourthly, Article 73 bis requirements; fifth, the Defence Pre-Trial brief; sixth, the trial date. There may be one or two other matters to consider as well. Before moving to the Prosecution motion for protective measures, I should comment on the lateness in starting the proceedings and to say that the Chamber does not wish this to be a precedent for the trial. The schedule time had been given and announced, and in future, the Chamber expects that arrangements will be made to ensure that we can start at the scheduled time. In respect of the first matter that I outlined, the Prosecution motion for protective measures, we have had the motion, and I'll just inquire from the Defence whether any Defence counsel have anything to say in relation to the motion. Yes, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: On behalf of the accused Todorovic, we take no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the same position is for Mr. Miroslav Tadic, as Mr. Brashich stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence of Milan Simic takes the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence of Simo Zaric also has the same position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it only remains then to inquire from the Prosecution whether they are requesting either a closed session or an open session with certain other protective measures, because that matter was left open in the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll ask my colleague, Ms. Paterson, to address that. She's been dealing with that part of the case, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the information currently available to us from our conversations with all but one of the witnesses on the list, we believe that they are willing to testify in open session, but they may request that their faces be disguised. There's one witness that we have not been able to make recent contact with, so I'm not able to state the position concerning that witness. It may be that that witness, who is a sexual assault victim, may want a closed session. But as far as we know, the vast majority of them, we can go in open session but perhaps with facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The motion is granted in the terms requested. But the question as to whether the witness will testify in open or closed session will be taken up immediately before the witness's testimony and a determination made. The next matter for consideration is the Prosecution motion for judicial notice. The last time when the Chamber was in session, this matter was left in the following state: The Prosecution and the Defence were to meet with a view to trying to agree on certain facts in respect of which, up to that time, there was no agreement. May I hear from the Prosecution first?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. Your Honours, in relation to three of the accused and their counsel, namely, the accused Mr. Tadic, Mr. Todorovic (sic), and Mr. Zaric, considerable progress has been made. The approach taken, Your Honours, was to deal firstly with -- well, firstly, there was a number of matters in the contested facts or adjudicated facts motion which had been agreed, and those matters went through and were settled. Secondly, the Defence had made some proposed amendments which the Prosecution considered, and a large number of those were accepted. Finally, Your Honours, there was a number of compromised proposals put forward to the Defence, and, by agreement, a large number of those were settled. Your Honours, if I said "Mr. Todorovic" had reached an agreement, I have misspoken. The three accused through which we have reached agreement are the accused Tadic, Simic, and Zaric. In relation to the accused Mr. Todorovic, we have been endeavouring to make contact with Mr. Brashich since the last occasion, and, indeed, on quite a number of occasions, attempts have been made to telephone him. Messages have been left. We have written him letters and faxes, but unfortunately we've been unable to contact him or to arrange any meetings with him. We are in the unfortunate position at the moment that with respect to three of the accused, we have substantial agreement on the adjudicated facts, but with one of the accused, Todorovic, we simply don't know what the position is. That would become very awkward at trial, Your Honours, because it would mean that in relation to three of the accused, no evidence is required between the three accused because they've agreed, but with relation to one accused, Mr. Todorovic, unless some sort of arrangement can be made, we would be leading all the evidence in relation to that. We're somewhat disappointed that we haven't been able to achieve some sort of consensus on these matters with Mr. Brashich, but all attempts to contact him have failed on our part, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: With regard to the attempts of being in contact with the Prosecution, I am sure that this Court can take judicial notice of what is right now happening in former Yugoslavia. I have been in the unfortunate position of being under time constraints in at least 21 cases where discovery cut-off schedules, because of the bombing in Yugoslavia, had been cut off, my ability to respond to prior outstanding orders. I have apologised to the Prosecution this afternoon, but it was, to a great extent, outside of my ability to respond to all demands by various judges. In addition, I have had two immediate members of my family die in the last 30 days, so I have been out of commission with regard to that. With regards to the judicial notice requests, I've gone over them, and, frankly, with a number of them, I am mystified as to what, if anything, they have to do with my client. Whether or not Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, I do not see relevance with regard to the indictment which my client stands accused of. I will endeavour, if my co-counsel have reached a consensus on these historical issues, I will most certainly go along with the consensus that, in 1908, Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, no doubt while you are here, the Prosecution would be in a position to take advantage of your presence and to carry out consultations. The Chamber requires that that be done. In any event, we will give both sides a period of two weeks in which to present us with a list of the agreed facts so that the Chamber will be in a position to make a determination on this issue once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter that we move to is the status of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. Can I say a few words, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On behalf of my colleagues, I would like to inform this Trial Chamber that our position is as follows because, unfortunately, our distinguished colleague, Mr. Brashich, is not fully aware and informed due to his personal problems and circumstances. I would like to draw the attention of this honourable Trial Chamber to the Prosecutor's motion dated February the 10th, then to Defence response of February 22nd. Following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Defence response, the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Defence response on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Following the good spirit of cooperation in previous parts of the proceedings, the Prosecutor's Office and my colleagues and me, we were able to open some discussions and to exchange some proposed matters. However, I would like to outline that we still stand very firmly in our relief requested by our response of February 22nd. We consider these facts not as adjudicated facts or facts of common knowledge. Finally, the Prosecutor's Office agreed with us in his letter dated April 27 that I will quote: "Please be advised that the Prosecution agrees to the following statements for the purposes only of the above matter before the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal." So to clarify, and I'm sure that my distinguished colleague, Mr. Niemann, also would agree with me, that only for the purposes of Rule 73 bis we have some agreements because the spirit of cooperation is our common interest, and procedural economy too. So, please, with regard to our other reliefs, we, as I said, absolutely we stand on a position that these facts could not be adjudicated or facts of common knowledge. Fortunately, following the reliefs and rulings by this same Trial Chamber based on a motion for judicial notice about the character in our response, we are quite familiar about the categories which kind of facts might be considered as adjudicated facts or facts of common knowledge, so now we are speaking strictly about the facts in terms of Rule 73. In addition, after a very profound and very detailed discussion and communication with the Office of the Prosecutor, we found, after carefully reviewing propositions provided to us by the Prosecutor, that some of the paragraphs do not correspond to our response. So for the judicial record, I would like to outline as follows: In Annex 1 of our response dated February 22nd, the Defence gave its statement of non-contested matters of fact. In Chapter A, in Chapter B, with paragraphs almost 60 and 68 or 65, I don't know, we didn't find -- we didn't find some of these paragraphs in the proposal of the Prosecutor. So maybe it's a mistake in correspondence or whatever. So for judicial record, the Defence would like to outline that all paragraphs mentioned in its response of 10th of February should be considered as a non-contested matter of fact in terms of Rule 73. In addition, we have noticed that some of the proposed and discussed issues were not properly mentioned in correspondence sent to us by the Prosecutor, although we have agreed upon some facts and we have discussed it in detail. This is paragraph number 3 in your letter of yesterday about the percentage of the statistics, et cetera. Probably it's a typewriting mistake. And especially there is a mistake in your paragraph (a)(16) speaking about the nature and scope of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia which the Defence, by its letter sent to the Office of the Prosecutor, basically is changed, and now we found actually genuine and basic terms that you proposed in your motion. So, in short, the Defence absolutely agree with the dateline proposed by the Trial Chamber and ordered by the Trial Chamber. In this time, we shall do our best in, I would say, clarifying some technical mistakes or correspondence mistakes, and we shall find a way to inform the Trial Chamber, probably by joint motion, with regard to these facts in a spirit of Rule 73 bis. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any other counsel for the Defence wish to say anything on this matter? If not, I shall just reiterate the ruling of the Trial Chamber on this issue, which is that within two weeks, the Prosecution and the Defence will present the Chamber with a statement as to those facts in respect of which there is agreement, and I would like to assure Mr. Pantelic that the decision of the Chamber will be reasoned and will, of course, take due account of all the submissions that have been made, including those made today. We now move to the next matter, which is the status of disclosure of witness statements, and I would just ask Mr. Niemann to inform us as to the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We have disclosed all statements of witnesses that we intend to call in the proceedings both in the English language and in the language of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does any counsel for the Defence wish to make any comment or observation on this? If not, let us seize the agreement and move on to the next matter, which is Article 73 bis requirements. The first matter is the pre-trial brief from the Prosecution, which is at hand. The second matter, as to admissions by the parties, that would be affected by the question of judicial notice. In respect of that, does any counsel wish to say anything? Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apprehend that the admission and statement about other matters not in dispute would largely be covered by the adjudicated fact issue. I don't expect, Your Honours, that it would cover every issue, and I would consider that we may need also to address that as a separate matter by way of perhaps the Prosecution putting to the Defence questions as to which matters are in dispute and which aren't. This is something which may assist in reaching some sort of status on that so that we know what's in dispute and what's not. I think that the adjudicated facts motion would cover most of it, but there may be other matters which aren't resolved by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does any counsel for the Defence wish to say anything on that? Mr. Niemann, these other matters which may be affected, which may be included but which are not specifically covered by judicial notice, you are not in a position now to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The position is that it is largely affected by the judicial notice part of the process, and we only basically reached agreement yesterday or the day before yesterday on that question, so it's only come in very recently. What I envisage is one would need to look at the indictment and compare it with the facts which are agreed and then determine what matters are still outstanding, having looked at the indictment, to determine what matters are in dispute and what matters are not contested, and that's a process which we will have to do once we reach agreement upon the question of facts. So it seems to me, Your Honours, that at least with Mr. Brashich, we are in no position at this stage to take into consideration any question of facts. After we have our meeting with him, we can do that. With the other accused, where we have made much further progress, we're certainly much closer to being able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Unlike the issue of judicial notice, the accused Todorovic has pleaded innocent in this matter, and by the fact that he has pleaded innocent in this particular matter, all of the factual allegations in the indictment -- and I specify the indictment -- have been put in play. So with regard to that issue, I do not and cannot, at this particular point in time, agree as to any facts which are alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We take note of that, you join issue with -- with everything. I think the best course for this is that at the end of the two weeks that the Chamber has given in respect of judicial notice, the Prosecution will then be in a position to give us a statement as to the matters on which there is agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's certainly, I think, the best course, Your Honours. Might I inquire through Your Honours whether Mr. Brashich will be in The Hague next week because, I mean, this is a process which will take some time. If he doesn't intend to be here, I don't see us making much progress, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: My plans were to spend Friday, tomorrow, and Saturday here in The Hague either with consultations with the Prosecution and more specifically in consultations with my client. I was not aware that tomorrow is a legal holiday. I was made aware of that when I arrived here today. If necessary, within the next two weeks, I will come back and meet with the Prosecutor. But to go back to the issue at hand as I see it, Your Honour, the Rule is somewhat unclear, and, of course, I don't know whether or not it has been discussed in any one of the decisions. Rule 73 bis (B)(ii): "... admissions by the parties and a statement of other matters which are not in dispute." I take it that we are discussing this issue. If the fact is that my client, Mr. Todorovic, was born on such and such a date, yes, of course, we can have an admission as to that particular fact. If we have a request for an admission that Bosanski Samac is located at a certain latitude and a certain longitude, I'm sure that we can agree to that. But again I reiterate that every factual allegation against my client, by the entry of a not guilty plea, is put into play, and the burden is upon the Prosecution to prove to the satisfaction of this Trial Chamber the allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're not endeavouring to avoid our burden, we are merely trying to comply with the Rules, and the Rules are drafted in this way, whereas, as a pre-trial process, to endeavour to eliminate any matters which need not be contested at the trial. Your Honours, it's encouraging to hear that there are at least some matters that Mr. Brashich is prepared to admit to, perhaps there are more, and I believe that a meeting with him at some date over the period of the next two weeks may be helpful in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, perhaps I'm misreading the Rule. The Rule specifically authorises the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecutor, not the Defence, to file an admission by the parties, and there is no admission by my client, and a statement of other matters that are not in dispute. It is the Prosecution's burden, if the Court so finds, to direct the Prosecution to do so. This is not a joint effort the way I read the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the Rule is sufficiently clear on its face. For the Prosecution to discharge the responsibility which the Chamber will place on it, it will be necessary for the Prosecution to be in communication with the Defence to ascertain those matters in respect of which there can be agreement. I would just like to reiterate that on this matter, the Prosecutor should endeavour to meet with Mr. Brashich and see to what extent they will be in a position to discharge the duty that the Chamber has placed on them within two weeks. I think they should endeavour to take advantage of your presence here, and it is a matter for you to say to the Prosecutor exactly what you have said here. I really don't see that this is a very complicated issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter for consideration is a statement of contested matters of fact and law, which is the converse of the issue that we just looked at. Mr. Niemann, do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, other than those matters which I have already put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does any counsel from the Defence wish to say anything on that? We will move on. We come now to Rule 73 bis (B)(iv): "(iv) a list of witnesses the Prosecutor intends to call with: (a) the name or pseudonym of each witness." That has been complied with. "(b) a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify." That has been complied with. "(c) the points in the indictment as to which each witness will testify." That has been done in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. "(d) the estimated length of time required for each witness." That has been complied with. The Chamber has some comments on the last matter, but before making those comments, I just inquire whether any counsel wish to say anything on any of those four points. Mr. Niemann, on the question of the estimated length of time, you have, in fact, offered an estimate as to the time that each witness will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I imagine that by aggregating those hours, one would arrive at an estimate of the aggregate. Would you like to tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Might I consult, Your Honour? I'm sorry, Your Honours. Your Honours, we haven't actually ever sat down and added them up, but our estimate was that it would take six to eight weeks for the Prosecution witnesses to testify based on the number of witnesses that we intend to call, that's the 60-odd witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you whether the estimate that you have given is confined to examination-in-chief or whether it includes an estimate as to cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The estimate that we have provided for in our summaries was an estimate of the Prosecution time for testimony. The eight-week period would be a period of time allowed for cross-examination, but I am hesitant to be too certain about this. I say this because, Your Honours, (a) we don't know for sure just how long cross-examination is going to take, and (b), when there is four accused, the process of cross-examination is always much lengthier than what you can reasonably estimate. So there is some allowance in the eight-week period for cross-examination, and we would endeavour to see if we could complete it in that time, but I wouldn't want to be held to that, Your Honours. It really is a matter that the Defence would have to address and perhaps give their estimate too. To put it another way, I would imagine it would take no more than six weeks in chief for the Prosecution case to present its evidence, but that wouldn't be allowing for cross-examination. I don't know whether that's much assistance to Your Honour, but my experience in these matters is when there is multiple accused, the cross-examination in some cases can be very lengthy, and, of course, there is nothing the Prosecution can do about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. My best mathematics produce the following result: From the witnesses that you have identified, there would be a total of about 183 hours. That doesn't include the witnesses that would take more than a day, of which there are six. Four would take two days, in your estimation; one, a day and a half; and one, one day. In terms of the standards of this Tribunal, this ought to be seen as a relatively short case, and we should endeavour to ensure that it is as brief as possible having, of course, regard to the interests of justice. The Chamber would encourage you, Mr. Niemann, where you have witnesses who will be testifying for a long time or, in any event, where witnesses testify to a particular event, to consider whether there is a need for repetition, and to the extent that that can be avoided without prejudicing your case, we would encourage you to take that approach. There's one other matter on this question. You haven't yet provided a sequence as to the witnesses, the order in which they will testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's true. We can, of course, and will, of course, do that if Your Honours wish us to do it. Our position on it depends a bit on whether or not it's easier to bring some witnesses from the former Yugoslavia, having a regard to the current situation, or to take them from other places. That's a matter which has been exercising our minds in relation to that process. But if the trial date is set and Your Honours wish for us to file an order of witnesses at some period of time prior to that, I'm sure that we can comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the Chamber considers that it is more than useful and it will facilitate its work, not only its work but the work of the Defence as well, to have filed a list as to the sequence in which witnesses will give their testimony. In this regard, the Chamber will require that this be done no later than three weeks before the date that we will set for trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. There's no difficulty with that. The reason I raise the difficulty is because Your Honours are aware of the fact that the war at the moment has restricted movement in the whole of Yugoslavia. It's not just in Serbia. In fact, movement of people in and out, witnesses and so forth, has become extremely difficult. That was the reason why we hadn't settled on any matter. But certainly three weeks would be adequate, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter for consideration is the Prosecutor's list of exhibits, and that has been filed. Is there any comment from any Defence counsel on that? I turn next to the Defence pre-trial brief. The Chamber has considered this matter and will require that the Defence pre-trial brief be filed by the end of May. I turn next to the trial date. Having given consideration to all the matters that we have discussed and considered, the Chamber will set a date of June the 22nd as the commencement date, that's a Tuesday, until the 14th of July for the first sittings. Thereafter, the Chamber will determine the dates as it is convenient. Note that June the 22nd is a Tuesday. There is one other matter that we have to consider. Mr. Niemann, the accused Blagoje Simic is not present, and it seems likely that he will not be present for trial, but he's on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I wish to inquire what course the Prosecution intends to take in respect of that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, the course that was taken in the Tadic case in relation to this was that -- he was charged with another accused. The indictment in that case wasn't amended. The indictment simply lay on file. We proceeded with the Prosecution that Mr. Tadic learned, and at the end of the day, there was no finding, of course, in relation to the accused whose name was Mr. Borovnica. That was the decision taken in that case. I have in mind that there was in other cases an amendment made to the indictment so that the name of the accused was removed and proceeded by separate indictment. Your Honours appreciate that we must keep the indictment alive. We simply can't ask you to dismiss it in relation to that accused. It probably is tidier to just allow the name to lay on file, for the indictment to be alive in relation to that accused, and for the trial will proceed against these accused. Your Honours will be asked to make no finding in relation to that accused. I am in Your Honours' hands. If we have to prepare a separate indictment, we will be pleased to do that, but we would have to have two indictments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, we have given consideration to this matter of Mr. Blagoje Simic, who is not present and is not likely to be present. We have considered the course that you have suggested of leaving him on the indictment and then the Chamber not making a finding in respect of him. The Chamber is not in favour of that approach. The trial should proceed without Mr. Blagoje Simic being on the indictment, and the Prosecution must take the necessary measures to ensure that he's not on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to that, may I just mention something? If Your Honours wish us to file another indictment, we can certainly take steps to do that. Might we ask that we not be required to do it until the morning of trial? I say that because, A, it won't cause any prejudice to the other accused, but, B, if this accused does, in fact, turn up between now and that date, we don't want to be in a position where we then have to seek a compound of the indictment because we would have severed the indictment. If Your Honours wish us to file a fresh indictment, we can do it, but if we can just leave it to the day of commencement of the trial, we would be most grateful in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no difficulty with that. It can be done the day of the commencement of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just return to the dates set for trial? I had given the dates Tuesday, June 22nd to the 14th of the July. That will be affected by the meeting of the Plenary which is scheduled for -- I'm just getting the dates of the Plenary. The Plenary is the 30th of June to the 2nd of July. On those dates, there will be no sittings. Mr. Niemann?
